thread:
maria: heads up — eu-west serving pool is saturated right now. streaming p99 is ~2.4s and backlog queue for streaming models is >120. non-stream requests still flow through but we're seeing long tail and timeouts for live sessions. anyone else seeing this?

chris: saw it. admission controller currently biases for throughput (non-streaming) so streaming sessions which keep GPU sessions + kv caches open end up blocking slots. we set streaming weight to 1 but that doesn't capture long-lived socket occupancy.

sam: can you paste admission metrics? queue length, active_sessions, avg_kv_bytes?

maria: pasting quick prometheus query snapshot:```
admission_queue_length{pool="eu-west",mode="stream"} 124
admission_active_sessions{pool="eu-west",mode="stream"} 88
admission_active_sessions{pool="eu-west",mode="sync"} 210
gpu_utilization{pool="eu-west"} 0.78
kv_cache_bytes{model="gpt-open-7b"} 4.1e9
```

chris: thanks. two things: 1) our rate-limits are rps-based per model; streaming should be charged/constrained on concurrency tokens instead, because an open stream is holding resources for duration. 2) streaming requests often disable batching or force batch size=1 which hurts throughput for other workloads — admission needs headroom-aware balancing.

jay: also, noticed NIC queue drops in az-2 earlier which increases latency on chunked frames, so streams hang longer and reclaim timers don't fire. networking + admission compounding the backlog.

deploy-bot: scheduled: canary rollout of admission concurrency-mode to eu-west at 2026-03-18T15:00:00Z (will run 10% nodes for 20m then expand)

maria: proposed immediate mitigation: 1) flip streaming to consume "concurrency_token" per open stream (limit = ceil(0.8 * pool_capacity_units)) 2) enforce max_stream_duration=120s for non-enterprise tenants and soft-close after 90s with warning 3) lower streaming batch window to 20ms / batch_size cap 4) add preemptive reclaim for low-priority streams after idle threshold 60s.

sam: we should also run a cost sim — streaming occupancy multiplies GPU-hours. for customers with high sustained streams, dedicated streaming pools or dedicated instances will be cheaper and simpler. put that in the proposal.

chris: I'll draft the canary config and a headroom-rebalance script that periodically computes streaming_capacity = floor(0.8 * total_tokens - active_sync_tokens) and exposes it to admission. quick config snippet:```yaml
admission_policy:
  mode: concurrency
  concurrency_limits:
    streaming: "$STREAM_LIMIT"
    sync: "$SYNC_LIMIT"
  preemption:
    enabled: true
    reclaim_after: 60s
```

maria: perfect. once canary is up let's watch p50/p95/p99 and queue depth for 30m before expanding. canary rollout should also include NIC error metrics so we can correlate network-induced stalls. :thumbsup:

jay: noted — i'll add NIC drop alerts to the canary dashboard and add a small synthetic streaming workload to exercise handshake/keepalive behavior.

maria: thanks team — timeline: canary in 1h, evaluate 30m, then iterate. if we can't stabilize, next step is dedicated streaming pool for top-tier customers.
